newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NAMIBIA BUDGET POSITIVE BUT SPEND TOO HIGH - REPORT.
newsitem.headline: NAMIBIA BUDGET POSITIVE BUT SPEND TOO HIGH - REPORT.

text.p: Namibian Finance Minister Nangolo Mbumba's maiden budget, unveiled on Wednesday, should pave the way for improved growth, although tougher action is needed on public spending, South Africa's Standard Bank said.

"The budget delivered on March 5 can be characterised as a holding one. Although the budget remains stimulatory it is less stimulatory that previous budgets," the bank's economics division said in a report.
Standard said the spread between current and capital spending was good but more boldness was needed in cutting overall expenditure.
"Government's spending as a share of GDP, at 48.1 percent, is too high, and needs to be brought down as rapidly as possible, to below 30 percent," it said.

The point was acknolwedged by Mbumba who said that while Namibia was on course to achieve a budget deficit target of about three percent of GDP by the year 2000, it still suffered the burden of a bloated public sector.
For the current year, Mbumba said the government was expecting a deficit of not more than 3.7 percent.
After a tough 1996, Standard said this year should see some consolidation in the Namibian economy, which is benefiting from the best rains in years.
Hopes for the longer-term depended crucially on the success of the Export Processing Zone programme, designed to reduce Namibia's dependence on the primary sector, the bank added.
So far Namibia has processed 20 applications involving N$150 million from companies interested in establishing EPZ operations.
